key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can introduce subtle data leakage into protein–protein interaction (PPI) inference pipelines, causing artificially inflated performance metrics that overstate real predictive ability.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes how using pretrained pLM embeddings can leak dataset-specific information into PPI models, exposing a blind spot in common evaluation practices.
method: Systematic empirical analysis comparing PPI inference results with and without pLM-derived features to isolate the effect of pretrained embeddings.
Controlled experiments and evaluation splits designed to reveal leakage-driven performance gains vs. genuine generalization.
Quantification of performance inflation and recommendations for stricter data-splitting and validation protocols to avoid misleading results.
impact: Alerts ML practitioners that off-the-shelf pLM features can mask true model performance on PPI tasks, prompting more rigorous evaluation standards to ensure reliable biological predictions.
visual_elements: Schematic showing how pretrained embeddings can carry information from training/related sequences into downstream PPI predictors (arrow from pLM to leakage icon).
Bar chart comparing reported (inflated) vs. corrected performance scores across models with and without pLM features.
Flowchart of recommended evaluation protocol (dataset split → leakage checks → model training → unbiased evaluation).
Warning/alert icon paired with checklist: data-split controls, sequence-similarity filtering, ablation tests.
paper_title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
